memoryText: If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Daniel 3:17-18 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
These words were spoken by three young men facing death. They stand at the center of the book of Daniel, and they define what faithfulness looks like when the stakes are highest.

“Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us.” The first statement is about God’s ability. They do not doubt that he can save them. They believe in a God who is powerful enough to rescue from a furnace seven times hotter than normal. They call him “our God whom we serve,” because their relationship is one of service. It is a statement of confidence.

“And he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.” The second statement is of expectation. They think God will rescue them. They are not stoic, bracing for the worst. They hope in God.

“But if not.” These two words are among the most powerful in Scripture. They show that their faith is not conditional. If God does not rescue them, their obedience stands. They do not make their loyalty depend on getting what they want from God. Their faith is in God himself, not in his rescue.

“Be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods.” The conclusion is a clear statement of allegiance. They do not argue about the details of the law. They simply refuse. And what follows is the rescue, with the fourth figure in the fire.

For the Christian, this is a model of faith in uncertain times. We pray for deliverance, believe that God can, and believe that he will. And we commit to obey in either case. Say this verse when you face a situation where the outcome is unknown. The God who is able is also with you in the fire.
weekInReview: This week you finished the last chapters of Ezekiel and began the book of Daniel. You prayed Psalms 128, 129, 131, 133, and 134, with their blessing of home and unity, their quiet trust, and their night blessing. In Ezekiel, you heard the watchman renewed, God’s promise to be the shepherd himself, the new heart and the Spirit within, the dry bones that lived, the final defeat of Gog, and the vision of the glory returning to a new temple. You read the river flowing from the sanctuary and bringing life to the Dead Sea, and the book’s last words: “The LORD Is There.” Then you met Daniel: the young man who would not defile himself, the dream of the statue and the stone, the three men in the fiery furnace, and the proud king humbled. Psalms 135 and 136 closed the week with God’s sovereignty over idols and his steadfast love that endures forever. The week taught that God himself will make his people new, that he dwells among them, and that faithfulness in exile is possible.
reflectionQuestions: Ezekiel’s river grows deeper as it flows, giving life to the Dead Sea. What place in your life or community needs God’s river of life?
Daniel and his friends lived faithfully in a foreign empire. What are the “Babylonian” pressures in your life, and what would faithful, gracious resistance look like?
The three men said, “But if not.” How does that kind of faith, not dependent on the outcome, challenge or comfort you?
prayerPrompts: Tell God that he is able to deliver you.
Thank him that he walks with you in the fire.
